summary: Conditional statements in Java allow a program to make decisions and execute different blocks of code based on whether a condition is true or false.
shortNotes: if statement runs a block only when its condition is true.
if-else gives two paths: one for true, one for false.
else-if ladder checks multiple conditions one by one.
switch statement matches a variable against several fixed values (cases).
Logical operators && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT) combine or negate conditions.

detailed.explanation:
A **conditional statement** lets your program choose what to do based on a condition. Instead of always running the same code from top to bottom, your program can ask a question like "Is the user's age above 18?" and take different actions depending on the answer.

The simplest form is the `if` statement. You write a condition inside parentheses; if it evaluates to `true`, the block inside the curly braces runs. If it is `false`, that block is skipped entirely.

An `if-else` statement adds a second block that runs when the condition is `false`. This gives you exactly two paths. When you need more than two paths, you chain `else if` blocks together — Java checks each condition from top to bottom and runs the first one that is `true`. Any remaining `else` block acts as a default.

The `switch` statement is a cleaner alternative when you are comparing one variable against many specific constant values (like integers or characters). Each `case` label matches a possible value, and a `break` statement stops execution from falling into the next case. A `default` case handles values that do not match any label.

Choosing the right conditional structure makes code easier to read and maintain. Use `if-else` for range checks or complex boolean expressions, and prefer `switch` when matching a single variable to a list of exact values.

definitions.meaning: A boolean expression that evaluates to either true or false, used to control which code block runs.
A conditional statement that executes a block of code only when its condition is true.
A conditional structure that executes one block if the condition is true and another block if it is false.
A chain of if and else-if blocks used to test multiple conditions sequentially.
A conditional statement that compares a single variable to multiple constant case values and executes the matching block.
A keyword used inside a switch block to stop execution from continuing into the next case.
The optional last case in a switch statement that runs when no other case matches.
An operator such as ==, !=, <, or > that compares two values and returns a boolean result.

points: Always use == to compare values in conditions, not = (which is assignment).
Curly braces {} are optional for a single-statement body, but always using them prevents bugs.
In an else-if ladder, only the first matching condition executes; the rest are skipped.
switch works with byte, short, int, char, String, and enum types — not with float or double.
Forgetting break in a switch causes fall-through: execution continues into the next case.
The default case in switch does not have to be last, but placing it last is best practice.
Logical AND (&&) requires both conditions to be true; logical OR (||) requires at least one to be true.
Exam tip: Trace code step-by-step, evaluating each condition with the given values to predict output.

commonMistakes: Using = (assignment) instead of == (comparison) inside a condition, e.g., writing if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5). Java will give a compile error for boolean contexts, but it is a very common confusion for beginners.
Forgetting the break statement in a switch case, causing fall-through where execution continues into the next case and prints unexpected output.
Writing conditions in the wrong order in an else-if ladder, such as checking score >= 60 before score >= 90, which causes higher grades to never be reached because a lower condition matches first.

questions.prompt: Which keyword is used to provide a default block in a switch statement when no case matches?
questions.explanation: The 'default' keyword in a switch statement marks the block that runs when none of the case values match the variable being tested.
x is 10, which is greater than 5, so the if block executes and prints A. The else block is skipped.

questions.prompt: Which of the following data types CANNOT be used directly in a switch statement in Java?
questions.explanation: Java's switch statement does not support floating-point types like double or float. It supports int, char, String, byte, short, and enum.

questions.prompt: In an else-if ladder, if the second condition is true, what happens to the remaining else-if blocks?
options: They are all checked as well.
questions.explanation: Once a matching condition is found in an else-if ladder, its block executes and all subsequent else-if and else blocks are skipped.

questions.prompt: What will happen if you omit the break statement in a switch case in Java?
options: Execution falls through to the next case.
questions.explanation: Without break, Java continues executing the statements in the following case(s) — this is called fall-through behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which logical operator returns true only when BOTH conditions are true?
questions.explanation: The && operator (logical AND) requires both operands to evaluate to true before the whole expression is true.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an if-else statement and a switch statement. When would you prefer to use switch?
questions.answer: An if-else statement evaluates any boolean expression and supports ranges or complex conditions, while a switch statement compares a single variable against fixed constant values. You prefer switch when you have many exact values to match for a single variable, such as day numbers or menu options, because it is cleaner and easier to read than a long else-if ladder.
questions.explanation: This question tests the student's understanding of when each conditional structure is appropriate, which is a common exam question.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to use == instead of = when writing a condition in an if statement in Java?
questions.answer: The = operator is the assignment operator; it sets a variable's value. The == operator is the equality comparison operator; it checks whether two values are equal and returns a boolean result. Using = inside a condition would attempt an assignment rather than a comparison, which causes a compile error in most boolean contexts in Java.
questions.explanation: Confusing = and == is one of the most frequent beginner mistakes in Java and many other languages.

questions.prompt: Write a Java program that reads an integer variable called 'temperature' (set it to any value you like). Using an if-else-if ladder, print 'Hot' if temperature is above 35, 'Warm' if it is between 20 and 35 (inclusive), and 'Cold' if it is below 20.
questions.explanation: First condition checks if temperature is strictly above 35 — if true, prints Hot. The else-if checks if temperature is 20 or above (we already know it is not above 35 at this point, so this covers 20 to 35) — prints Warm. The final else catches everything below 20 — prints Cold. With temperature set to 28, the output is Warm.

steps.say: Welcome! Today we are learning about conditional statements in Java. These let your program make decisions, just like you do in real life.
Think of it this way: if it is raining, you carry an umbrella, otherwise you don't. Your program works the same way.

write.content:
Program chooses code to run
based on a condition (true/false)

steps.say: A condition is just a question that has a yes or no answer, which in Java we call true or false.
The simplest conditional is the if statement. Let's write one. We have a variable age set to 20.
We write if, then the condition in round brackets, then the code to run inside curly braces.
If age is 18 or more, this line runs. Because 20 is greater than 18, Java prints you are an adult.
Now we add an else block. If the condition is false, Java runs the else block instead. So we get exactly two paths.
When you have more than two choices, you chain else-if blocks. Java checks each condition from top to bottom and runs the first one that is true.
Here we check a student score. If score is 90 or above, grade A. Else if 75 or above, grade B. Otherwise grade C.
The switch statement is great when you compare one variable to many exact values. Each case is one possible value, and break stops it from running into the next case.
Here is a very common mistake. Using a single equals sign inside a condition is assignment, not comparison. Always use double equals for comparison.
Another mistake is forgetting break in a switch case. Without it, execution falls through into the next case and prints extra output you did not expect.
